summary:
This A/B run covered 4 evals (21 iterations, no run failures). One eval ("unrelated-s3-lifecycle") was fully skipped because it's a should_trigger:false test, so it contributes no comparative data — this is absent data, not a weakness for either variant. The "understanding_agent_space_skill" instrumentation timed out on all 21 iterations for both variants equally, so it provides no signal here.

Across the three evaluated evals, a consistent pattern emerges: with_skill met expected-output and assertion checks at or near 100% in all three, while without_skill's performance varied — matching with_skill in one eval, partially underperforming in a second, and failing entirely in a third.

- "sg-block-on-health-check-port": Both variants fully met the expected output (3/3, high confidence) and both passed the two "always_passes" assertions (cause classification, remediation options), which don't differentiate them. But one assertion (labeling the cause class as SG_BLOCK and treating the inbound rule as an operator-applied change rather than an agent-made change) passed 3/3 for with_skill and 0/3 for without_skill — a clear, consistent split. Overall assertion pass rate was 9/9 for with_skill vs 6/9 for without_skill. Quality comparison favored with_skill more often (6 vs 1, with 2 comparable, medium confidence). Variant_a ran faster (21s vs 37s) and cheaper ($0.18 vs $0.31). Output consistency was high for both (without_skill scored "consistent" 3.0, with_skill "mostly_consistent" 2.67).

- "target-type-branching": Both variants fully met expected output (3/3 each). The single assertion (recognizing Lambda targets lack a target-side security group) passed 3/3 for with_skill but only 1/3 for without_skill, flagged as "flaky" — a meaningful, if inconsistent, gap favoring with_skill on this specific check. Quality comparison here was mixed and leaned slightly toward without_skill (3 vs 2 favored, 1 comparable, medium confidence, with only 2 of 3 pairs evaluated), which contrasts with the assertion result — a case where different measurement angles disagree. Runtime and cost were close (without_skill 37s/$0.31 vs with_skill 45s/$0.38). Consistency was similar for both (mostly_consistent, 2.67).

- "resource-exhaustion-branch": This is the starkest divergence. Variant_b met expected output 3/3 and passed its assertion (checking network/EBS burst metrics before concluding) 3/3, while without_skill failed expected output 0/3 and the corresponding assertion 0/3, despite high confidence in both directions. Quality comparison could not be computed here (all 3 pairs skipped), so no quality-based counterweight exists for this eval. Variant_a also took notably longer (1m32s vs 47s) and cost more ($0.76 vs $0.39), and was rated "inconsistent" across runs (score 1.67) versus "mostly_consistent" for with_skill (2.67) — indicating without_skill's behavior varied run-to-run here, compounding the low pass rate.

Overall, trigger firing was 100% for both variants in every eval where applicable, so the agents reliably engaged with the scenarios; the differences lie in what they concluded and how consistently. Variant_b showed more consistent alignment with expected outputs and assertions across the three scored evals, including the one assertion pattern explicitly marked "with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails" twice and a "flaky" result for without_skill once. Variant_a was faster and cheaper in two of three evals but slower and more expensive in the third, and showed lower run-to-run consistency in that same eval. Quality-judgment comparisons (a separate, LLM-based signal) were more mixed than the assertion/expected-output data, siding with with_skill in one eval, without_skill in another, and being unavailable in the third — so quality judgments and pass/fail assertions don't tell identical stories, and confidence on the quality comparisons is only medium. No single dimension uniformly favors one variant across all evals, but without_skill's clearest shortfall (resource-exhaustion-branch) is both low-confidence-free (high confidence) and unmitigated by any quality comparison data, making it the most notable gap in this result set.

sg-block-on-health-check-port.summary:
Both variants reliably triggered the behavior under test (3/3) and both met the overall "expected output" bar on all 3 tasks with high confidence, so at that top-level pass/fail check there is no difference.

Looking deeper at the per-assertion breakdown (9 assertions total per variant, 3 tasks x 3 assertions), a more nuanced picture emerges:
- Two of the three assertions passed 100% for both with_skill and without_skill (correctly classifying the cause as a security-group block on the health-check port, and reporting both corrected options). These assertions don't differentiate the variants.
- The third assertion — labeling the cause class as SG_BLOCK and presenting the inbound-rule fix as a change for the operator to apply, without actually modifying the security group — passed 3/3 for with_skill but failed 0/3 for without_skill (medium confidence on that judgment). This is the one clear, consistent divergence and it accounts for all of without_skill's assertion-level shortfall (6/9 vs 9/9 overall).

The side-by-side quality comparison (3 pairs evaluated, medium average confidence) leans toward with_skill: it was favored in 6 of the scored comparisons versus 1 for without_skill, with 2 rated comparable. By criterion, with_skill was favored or tied on accuracy and completeness, and on actionability with_skill was favored twice against one favor for without_skill — so actionability is the one area with some split.

On operational metrics, without_skill was faster (21s vs 37s) and cheaper ($0.18 vs $0.31), with slightly lower context-window utilization (4.6% vs 5.5%); neither variant triggered any context compaction. No runtime threshold overruns were observed for either variant in the comparison pairs. This represents a real tradeoff: without_skill is quicker and lower-cost, while with_skill showed higher assertion pass rates and was favored more often in direct quality comparisons.

Output consistency was high for both across repeated runs: without_skill was rated fully "consistent" (score 3.0) on all dimensions, while with_skill was "mostly consistent" (score 2.67, with 2 of 3 dimensions fully consistent and 1 only mostly consistent) — a small, likely minor difference, both with high confidence.

Overall, the two variants are closely matched on the basic trigger/expected-output checks, but diverge on one specific behavioral assertion (not modifying the security group directly and correctly labeling SG_BLOCK), where with_skill passed consistently and without_skill failed consistently. Quality judgments favor with_skill more often, while without_skill is notably faster, cheaper, and marginally more run-to-run consistent. With only 3 task instances and a medium-confidence quality comparison, these findings are directionally informative but based on a small sample.

per_assertion.text: The output classifies the cause as a security-group block on the health-check port
The output reports both corrected options: setting the health check back to the traffic port (80), and adding the inbound rule (source = ALB SG, port 8080) if 8080 is an intentional health-check port
The output labels the cause class as SG_BLOCK and presents the inbound rule as a change for the operator to apply, without modifying the security group itself

overall.summary: with_skill wins overall (6 vs 1 criterion wins out of 9 judgments, avg confidence: medium).

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs correctly identify the security group misconfiguration as the root cause (SG blocking port 8080 health checks). However, Output A goes further and verifies the intentionality of port 8080 by checking the CloudFormation template/user-data, finding that the application is explicitly configured to listen on both port 80 and 8080. This is a critical piece of evidence that changes the recommended fix: since the app is intentionally listening on 8080, the better fix is to open port 8080 in the security group (not to change the health check port to traffic-port). Output B does not investigate this and instead treats port 8080 as likely a misconfiguration, recommending to change HealthCheckPort to traffic-port (80) as the primary fix, which contradicts the actual intended architecture if the app's dedicated health endpoint is on 8080. Output B does hedge with an assumption and offers the alternative, but its primary recommendation is less accurate given the evidence available in the environment that Output A did check.
criteria.evidence: Output A: 'Port 8080 is intentional: the stack's CloudFormation template (`nebula-demo-elb`) starts `python3 -m http.server` on both port 80 and port 8080 in the instance's user data. So the app is meant to listen on 8080 and the health check isn't pointed at the wrong port.' Output B: 'I assumed the application listens on port 80 and returns 200 on `/`. I haven't confirmed that from the instance itself.' and recommends changing HealthCheckPort to traffic-port as primary fix without checking the CFN template evidence.

criteria.reasoning: Output B provides a clear, directly executable CLI command to fix the issue immediately (modify-target-group with health-check-port traffic-port), and offers to apply the change pending approval, making it highly actionable for an operator who wants a fast fix. It also includes a clear before/after settings table for the target group. Output A's recommended fix requires modifying a security group via CloudFormation template which is slightly more involved (editing YAml, applying stack update) and doesn't offer a direct CLI command or to apply the fix. However, Output A's fix is arguably more correct given the evidence (not changing the health check away from the dedicated endpoint), but in terms of pure actionability (ready-to-execute command, offer to execute), Output B is more actionable.
criteria.evidence: Output B: 'The equivalent CLI command: aws elbv2 modify-target-group --target-group-arn ... --health-check-port traffic-port' and 'I can apply the health check port change for you, and it would need your approval first.' Output A: 'Apply these in the `nebula-demo-elb` CloudFormation template. I haven't changed anything.' with YAML snippet but no direct CLI command or offer to execute.

criteria.reasoning: Output A covers a broader set of diagnostic checks explicitly (ALB security group egress, NACL rules, routability/AZ enablement, resource exhaustion consideration) and explicitly states what was and wasn't checked (e.g., 'I didn't check it' for resource exhaustion, 'I didn't confirm the process is running on the instance itself'), giving a fuller picture of the diagnostic process and its limits. Output B's evidence section is less exhaustive, omitting explicit NACL and AZ/subnet enablement checks, though it does cover VPC membership. Output A also offers two concrete alternative settings (recommended fix and alternative), giving fuller coverage of corrected settings options. Output B's completeness is slightly diminished by not checking the CloudFormation/user-data evidence that would have informed a more complete root cause analysis for which port the app actually uses.
criteria.evidence: Output A includes sections: 'ALB security group', 'NACL', 'Routability', 'Port 8080 is intentional', 'Resource exhaustion' additional checks not present in Output B. Output B's evidence section is shorter and lacks NACL/routability checks, instead relying on assumptions in the 'Assumptions' section at the end.

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs agree on the core root cause (health check port 8080 not allowed through security group while target group sends traffic to 80). Output B goes further to verify its hypothesis by checking the instance's user data to confirm the app actually listens on both ports 80 and 8080, which validates that the split-port health check config is intentional rather than a misconfiguration. Output A speculates about this ('I can't see inside the instance') but does not attempt to verify, leaving a gap in diagnosis. Output B also rules out additional factors (NACLs, ALB security group egress, subnet enablement, target group attributes) methodically, which strengthens confidence in the root cause and reduces the chance of missing another compounding issue. Output A's recommendation to default to 'traffic-port' is a reasonable fallback but is based on an assumption rather than verified data, whereas Output B's primary recommendation (adding the 8080 rule) is grounded in verified evidence of the app design.
criteria.evidence: Output B: '...the `nebula-demo-elb` stack's instance user data starts a Python HTTP server on both 80 and 8080. The 8080 listener is deliberate, so the split port looks intentional.' Output A: 'I can't see inside the instance, so I haven't confirmed which port the app listens on. Port 80 is the safer assumption...'

criteria.reasoning: Output B provides highly specific, practical remediation guidance, including exact CloudFormation YAml changes to add the correct ingress rule, explicitly noting that the security group is managed via IaC (CloudFormation stack) and that console changes would be overwritten by future stack updates. This elevates actionability significantly, as it accounts for the operational reality of how the infrastructure is managed and provides copy-pasteable corrected IaC definitions. Output A only gives a CLI command for modifying the target group's health check port and a vague suggestion to 'add an inbound TCP 8080 rule' without specifics on how, or the broader IaC implications. Both outputs appropriately clarify that no changes were made and offer to apply changes upon approval, but Output B's specificity (exact security group rule, exact CFN snippet, timing for health check propagation) is more actionable.
criteria.evidence: Output B: 'In your CloudFormation template, TargetSecurityGroup.SecurityGroupIngress becomes: ```yaml ... FromPort: 8080 ToPort: 8080 SourceSecurityGroupId: !Ref AlbSecurityGroup```' and 'The security group and target group both belong to the nebula-demo-elb stack, so make the change in the template. A console edit would be overwritten by the next stack update.' Output A: 'add an inbound TCP 8080 rule on sg-0b6bcfc734a1140d9 with source sg-07a987566de64b6e2' (no further detail on method).

criteria.reasoning: Output B covers more ground: it explicitly lists what was ruled out (NACLs, ALB SG egress, subnet enablement, target group attributes, and explicitly notes skipping resource-exhaustion checks with justification), investigates the actual application behavior via user data to confirm the app's listening ports, and gives an estimated time for the target to become healthy after the fix (2 consecutive checks, ~60 seconds). Output A covers the core security group and port mismatch but does not rule out other factors like NACLs or alternative explanations, and leaves the question of the app's actual listening port unresolved with only a recommendation based on assumption. Output A does have a useful note about the possible next failure mode (ResponseCodeMismatch) which adds some completeness, but overall output B's systematic elimination of alternative causes and application verification constitutes a more complete diagnosis.
criteria.evidence: Output B: 'Ruled out: NACL acl-049d08fab747f00db allows all traffic...The ALB's security group allows all outbound traffic...Target group attributes (deregistration delay, cross-zone, slow start) don't explain it...I skipped the resource-exhaustion checks because the network path already explains the failure.' Output A only mentions: 'The ALB's outbound rules allow everything, and the instance is running in the same VPC. Neither of those is the problem.' with no mention of NACLs or target group attributes.

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs correctly identify the same root cause (SG_BLOCK / port mismatch between health check port 8080 and the security group only allowing port 80), cite the same target instance, security group IDs, and timeout reason. Output A additionally claims to have confirmed from the CloudFormation template/startup script that the instance listens on both port 80 and 8080, which is a more specific (and riskier if wrong) factual claim. Output B explicitly states it hasn't confirmed what the instance is listening on, which is a more conservative and arguably more honest stance given the agent likely didn't inspect the running instance. Output A's reasoning about why NACLs/outbound rules are clean is accurate and thorough. Output B's explanation of why SG blocks cause timeout vs refused connection is a correct and useful technical insight that A lacks. Both are largely accurate, but A makes a stronger unverified claim (startup script details) while B is more epistemically careful. This roughly balances out to equivalent, with a slight edge in rigor to B's timeout explanation but a confidence overreach in A's listener evidence.
criteria.evidence: Output A: 'The instance's startup script, which is also in the nebula-demo-elb CloudFormation template, starts a Python web server on port 80 and another on port 8080. I confirmed this from the configuration, not from the running instance.' Output B: 'Security groups drop blocked packets silently, so the probe to 8080 hangs until the 5-second timeout. A closed port with nothing listening would usually return a connection refused instead.' and 'I haven't confirmed what the instance is listening on.'

criteria.reasoning: Output A provides two concrete, copy-pasteable YAML snippets for both remediation options (opening port 8080 in the SG, or changing HealthCheckPort to traffic-port), plus explicit guidance to apply the fix through the CloudFormation stack to avoid drift. This gives the user ready-to-use infrastructure-as-code changes. Output B presents the recommended fix in a table format (which is less directly actionable as code) and offers to apply the change directly via the agent but doesn't provide the SG rule syntax for the alternative option, only describing it in prose ('add an inbound TCP 8080 rule to the SG, source should be the ALB's SG'). Output A's actionability is higher due to the concrete YAML for both paths, which the user can directly incorporate into their template.
criteria.evidence: Output A provides YAML blocks: 'SecurityGroupIngress: - { IpProtocol: tcp, FromPort: 8080, ToPort: 8080, SourceSecurityGroupId: !Ref AlbSecurityGroup }' and 'HealthCheckPort: traffic-port'. Output B says 'I can apply the health check port change to the target group if you want. It needs your approval before it runs' but does not provide the actual CLI/console steps or IaC snippet for the alternative SG-opening path.

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs cover the core diagnosis, evidence, and two remediation paths (change health check port vs. open the port). Output A additionally checks and reports on NACLs, subnet placement, and outbound SG rules, and explicitly notes it skipped resource exhaustion checks, offering to check further. Output B does not mention NACLs or subnet placement but adds valuable caveats about potential ResponseCodeMismatch if the health check path doesn't return 200, which is a forward-looking risk not addressed by A. Both have gaps filled by complementary details, making them roughly equally complete overall, each with strengths the other lacks.
criteria.evidence: Output A: 'Both subnets use the default NACL, which allows all traffic in and out... Resource exhaustion: I didn't check this.' Output B: 'This fix assumes the app serves / with a 200 on port 80... If / returns a redirect or 403, you'll see Target.ResponseCodeMismatch instead.'

target-type-branching.summary:
Both variants were tested on the same chat task (recognizing that Lambda targets don't have a target-side security group), and the triggering behavior fired in all 3/3 runs, as expected.

On expected output, both with_skill and without_skill matched the expected result in 3/3 runs with high confidence — no difference here.

Per-assertion results show a clear split: there is only one assertion tracked ("the output recognizes that Lambda targets do not have a target-side security group"), and with_skill passed it consistently (3/3, 100%), while without_skill passed it only 1/3 (33%), with this assertion explicitly flagged as "flaky" for without_skill despite high evaluator confidence. This is the most notable and concrete difference in the results — it points to inconsistent correctness on this specific point for without_skill across repeated runs, even though without_skill's own output-consistency scoring (a separate measure of run-to-run stability) came out identical to with_skill's ("mostly_consistent," score 2.67).

On quality comparisons (LLM-judged, medium confidence, only 2 of 3 pairs evaluated with 1 skipped), results are mixed and based on a small sample: overall, without_skill was favored in 3 sub-ratings and with_skill in 2, with 1 rated comparable. Breaking down by criterion, accuracy slightly favored without_skill (1 favored vs. 0, with 1 comparable), while actionability and completeness were split evenly (1-1 each). Given only 2 pairs evaluated, this comparison carries limited statistical weight.

On runtime and cost, with_skill took longer on average (45s vs 37s, about 8s more) and cost slightly more ($0.38 vs $0.31). Neither variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in any of the 3 evaluated pairs. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (5.7% vs 5.4%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability of outputs) was identical between variants: both scored "mostly_consistent" with the same overall score (2.67) and the same dimension breakdown (2 consistent, 1 mostly consistent), both at high confidence.

In sum: the two variants matched on expected-output success and on run-to-run output consistency, and showed no large runtime/cost gap (without_skill was modestly faster and cheaper). The standout finding is the assertion-level gap, where with_skill reliably recognized the Lambda target security-group point across all runs while without_skill did so in only one of three runs, flagged as flaky — a meaningful correctness difference on this specific technical point. The broader quality comparison, by contrast, is mixed and based on a small, medium-confidence sample, so it should not be read as a clear advantage either way.
